articles.title_orig: Thousands Expected to Protest in France on Halloween: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Thousands Expected to Protest in France on Halloween: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Mark Landler and Ségolène Le Stradic
Hundreds of thousands of protesters were on the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, a now-weekly expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police, and kept the country on edge.
Adding to those fears: Halloween, which also falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.
In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired rounds of tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration in the city, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people had demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.
Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.
There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.
The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.
The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.
“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.
Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather in spite of the ban will lead to arrests, he said.
Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration in which public order is disrupted.
Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about the role played by social media in attracting people and inciting them to violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›
Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often end up in clashes with far-left groups.
Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›
Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.
I can hear loud bangs at the end of the demonstration route and I can see many people running backward, as well as tear gas in the distance. Some protesters are throwing mortar-like fireworks.
The mood at the Paris protest has definitely changed. Though I can still hear some protesters singing, the protest has turned violent.
Police officers are now blocking many of the roads in the neighborhood at the end of the demonstration route. I saw a young woman surrounded by medics — she was bleeding from the face. I saw flames at the end of one avenue. I also saw police officers charge toward the crowd. Some residents are trying to make their way back home quickly, covering their faces to avoid tear gas.
Tensions in Paris continue to rise. Police are skirmishing with 200 to 300 rioters who have refused to disperse at the end of a rally. The Paris police said the rioters threw Molotov cocktails and fireworks at officers. A car was set afire.
Tensions are now flaring between protesters and the police in Paris. Police are firing rounds of tear gas at people, who are refusing to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday.
The Interior Ministry estimated that 320,000 people took part in protests across the country today. That is somewhat fewer than last week (410,000) and the week before (550,000).
The demonstration in Paris remains peaceful, even festive. But police and protesters have clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes. Tear gas and water cannons have been deployed as the police try to disperse crowds. Violence typically breaks out at the end of these rallies, when people refuse to leave the scene.
I am walking along the authorized route for the demonstration in Paris. For the most part, the mood has been festive. Someone even dropped candy from his balcony, drawing cheers from the crowd.
After, I watched a half-dozen protesters dressed in black and wearing masks push trash bins in the middle of the crowd. One was already burning as they made their way, and they set the second on fire not far from where a police unit was stationed. Other demonstrators used water to put out the fire, causing a small clash with the ones wearing in black. “That’s no way to protest,” one of the demonstrators who put out the fire said.
The protest in Paris has a joyous and playful atmosphere. Brass bands are playing music, and many protesters have come dressed in Halloween costumes. Many said they wanted to help reverse the narrative set on Oct. 17 when riots spilled out of marches across France, leading to destruction and looting.
“I’m really worried about how the riots have been instrumentalized by the far right,” said Helen Olive, 50, who was among a group of parents who came dressed as “super parents.” “We want to turn that narrative around.”
Literature student Arthur Fleury, 20, arrived as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wore a mask of the far-right politician Marine Le Pen. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”
Early estimates from the French interior ministry suggest crowds are smaller today than the past two Saturdays. At 2 p.m., the ministry estimated that 15,000 people were taking part in 65 protests. That compares to 37,000 people last week at that time and 67,000 on Oct. 17. These numbers can be expected to grow as the day progresses. The ministry said it had arrested 27 people, compared with 217 by this time last Saturday. Protest organizers have yet to issue a crowd estimate; their numbers are typically far higher.
I’m at the Place de la Bastille. It is normally a bustling square, particularly on a beautiful, sunny Saturday. Now, police officers with shields and helmets patrol in groups. A loudspeaker blares a warning that gatherings and protests are forbidden to take place here by a police decree and that anyone who breaks it will be fined 135 euros.
Union and student organizers had again hoped to start their march here today, and again it was denied by the police and moved to the eastern edge of the city.
Mark Landler and Ségolène Le Stradic

articles.title_zh: Quad diplomats finalise first leaders’ summit in two years before Trump-Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
Without naming China, foreign ministers express ‘grave concerns’ about overcapacity disrupting global supply chains in critical industries.
Top diplomats from the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, or the Quad, met in Atlanta on Saturday to finalise preparations for next month’s summit in the Philippines, just weeks before US President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his counterparts from India, Japan and Australia on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) foreign ministers’ meeting, where they reaffirmed their commitment to a “free and open Indo-Pacific”.
Without naming China, the joint statement, released by Japan’s ministry of foreign affairs, expressed grave concerns over “overcapacity” and vowed to build “reliable and open global supply chains and trusted and resilient infrastructure”.

articles.title_orig: MAC details stark Taiwan-China divide
articles.title_zh: MAC details stark Taiwan-China divide
articles.content_orig:
The fifth plenum of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th Central Committee and Taiwan’s election debates highlighted a stark contrast between China’s centralization of power and Taiwan’s democracy, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said yesterday.
Differences in political systems are the most fundamental issue in cross-strait relations, which have nothing to do with similarities in culture, language or ethnicity, he said.
Shen made the remarks at a forum held by the Secure Taiwan Associate Corporation to discuss possible developments in China’s domestic political situation following the fifth plenum, and their implications for Taiwan.
Photo: Fang Wei-li, Taipei Times
The theme of the plenum, which concluded on Thursday last week, was “unswerving promotion of the full and rigorous party self-governance,” a move by Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) to further bolster the CCP’s leadership and consolidate his authority ahead of next year’s 21st CCP National Congress, Shen said.
The MAC’s analysis of the plenum can be summarized into four points, he said.
First, the “Xi Jinping thought on party building” was established as a political guiding principle, further consolidating Xi’s unchallengeable position as the party’s leader, Shen said.
The plenum confirmed earlier decisions to expel 33 officials from the party, including former senior military leaders Zhang Youxia (張又俠) and Liu Zhenli (劉振立), he said, adding that accusations against them, including failing to implement central policies and engaging in duplicity and disloyalty, demonstrated that anyone who is insufficiently loyal to Xi or deviates from his ideology and directives would be purged.
Second, the MAC believes that “strict party governance” aims to ensure the CCP’s long-term rule and preserve its one-party dictatorship, Shen said.
Whether it is political, organizational, integrity or work discipline, all rules must be based on monitoring and ensuring that party members and officials obey the CCP, he said, adding that the development of China’s constitutional system, and the protection of people’s rights and interests take a back seat to the goal of consolidating the CCP’s one-party rule.
Third, the promotion of “the party’s self-revolution” represents a rejection of external oversight by the public, media and civil society, Shen said.
Although the authenticity of posts that students from more than 10 Chinese universities had allegedly signed a petition calling for the abolition of the indefinite term for the president remains unverified, they signaled that the party’s leadership is not subject to any external oversight, he said.
Xi might respond to academic activities or social movements with further legal measures or intensified surveillance, he added.
The CCP has fully internalized its oversight mechanisms within the party’s disciplinary and supervisory systems, rejecting democratic checks and balances in the name of “self-correction within the party,” he said.
Fourth, moves to eliminate dissenting voices have paved the way for Xi to secure a fourth term at next year’s 21st National Congress, Shen said.
The number of Central Committee members and alternate members absent from the plenum reached a new high since the era of Mao Zedong (毛澤東), he said.
Large-scale purges of senior party, government and military officials over the past few years have removed potential political obstacles to Xi’s ambitions, ensuring he can continue on to a fourth term with the party’s full endorsement, he added.
While the plenum unfolded in Beijing, many in Taiwan were focused on the mayoral debates in Taipei and Kaohsiung, highlighting the fundamental differences between the political systems on the two sides of the Strait, Shen said.
The CCP’s fifth plenum demonstrated the consolidation of power and the growing dominance of Xi’s leadership, he said, adding that Taiwan’s lively mayoral debates would be impossible in China.
Shen urged Taiwanese to recognize these institutional differences and unite against authoritarian aggression, build a shared commitment to protecting freedom, democracy and national sovereignty to ensure that Taiwan can continue to  deepen its democracy, prosperity and development amid the CCP’s multifaceted pressure campaign.
With local elections entering their final campaign phase, the government would continue to closely monitor developments within the CCP and shifts in its power structure, while preventing and exposing various forms of Chinese election interference, he said.
It will also continue to counter China’s cognitive warfare, transnational repression and attempts to infiltrate and divide Taiwanese society, while defending national sovereignty, freedom, security and the democratic way of life, he added.

articles.title_orig: China’s military purge reduces war risk: experts
articles.title_zh: China’s military purge reduces war risk: experts
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) military purge has reduced the risks of a planned war against Taiwan, yet increased the danger of a conflict sparked by a miscalculation or accident, Taiwanese experts said yesterday.
They made the comments at a seminar on the Fifth Plenary Session of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th Central Committee held by the research group Secure Taiwan Associate Corp (STA) in Taipei.
The wholesale sacking of Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) officers and managers of the aerospace and defense industry is sure to set back Xi’s timetable to prepare the PLA to launch an invasion of Taiwan by next year, they said.
The Chinese armed forces’ attention would most likely be fully absorbed by efforts to rebuild their organization and leadership in the next one to four years in a welcome development for Taiwan, they said.
Yet the lack of experience in the Chinese military’s most senior command levels is also a warning sign, as amateurs and sycophants are far more likely to make missteps that inadvertently lead to war, they added.
Association for Strategic Foresight researcher Chieh Chung (揭仲) said that 96 CCP Central Committee members, or 26 percent of the total membership, have departed under a cloud.
This figure is more than double the number of Central Committee officials ousted for corruption or improprieties in the 18th iteration of the Central Committee, he said.
The dismissal of Ma Xingrui (馬興瑞), Jin Zhuanglong (金壯龍), Zhao Xiaozhe (趙曉哲) and Lei Fanpei (雷凡培), among 28 formerly high-ranking defense and aerospace industry officials, would force a comprehensive re-examination of China’s defense procurement plans, he said.
The drastic changes would derail the military reform targets Xi originally planned to achieve by the 100th anniversary of the PLA’s founding next year, he said.
Xi had rolled back the theater commands’ autonomy and ability to conduct operations independently, which runs contrary to recognized principles of modern joint warfare, he said.
The disruption to PLA leadership and its cumbersome command arrangements are likely to cripple the capability of the Chinese military to project force or respond to a contingency for the next three to four years, he said.
Yet, Xi’s willingness to put ideology and politics over professionalism also means Chinese generals would be fearful of voicing disagreements or appearing weak, he said.
These flaws would make it significantly more difficult for Beijing to exercise sound judgement or de-escalate dangerous situations, increasing the risks of sparking an unwanted conflict, he said.
The most recently dismissed members and alternate members of the Central Committee included 16 PLA brass and seven high-ranking managers of China’s defense industry, National Taiwan University political science professor Chen Shih-min (陳世民) said.
The PLA’s organizational table calls for more than 40 full generals and admirals to staff the armed forces, but only six such officers are left at the helm, he said.
The arrest of former vice chairman and PLA general Zhang Youxia (張又俠) nine months ago has all but eliminated the Central Military Commission, where he previously served as one of its two vice chairmen, Chen said.
The only members left in the Chinese military’s high command are Xi and General Zhang Shengmin (張升民), a commissar with no professional training in commanding troops, he said.
National Defense University Chinese military studies professor Ma Chen-kun (馬振坤) said the PLA would be absorbed by efforts to recuperate and reorganize its internal organization for up to two years.
The Central Committee meeting elevated Zhang Shengmin, the Central Military Commission’s last remaining general, to the Politburo, without filling vacancies in the high command, he said.
The prominence of Zhang Shengmin contravened the PLA’s long-standing policy of maintaining separate tracks for commissars and professional soldiers, he said.
Zhang Shengmin’s lack of qualifications have compromised the Chinese military’s crisis management, increasing the chances of dangerous miscalculations and mishaps, Ma said.
Starbucks Taiwan’s decision to charge for drink customization, which had been free, has sparked consumer backlash, highlighting the challenge of raising prices without making customers feel they are losing value, experts said.
Since Oct. 12, customers who order drinks with less or no ice and ask to have the volume topped up with milk or other liquid have been charged an additional NT$15.
Topping off drinks without ice was previously free, and disgruntled customers posted photos on social media showing that iced drinks ordered without ice were only half full if the extra NT$15 was not paid.
The posts drew tens of thousands

articles.title_orig: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore. Here are 6 new account takeover threats
articles.title_zh: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore. Here are 6 new account takeover threats
articles.content_orig:
Experts now say passkeys like biometrics and face ID are now the best way to protect our digital lives.
You may think of a stolen password as the main way someone gets into your account. But online criminals have learned that they do not always need to steal the password itself. They may hijack an active login session, convince you to approve a sign-in, take control of your phone number or use malware to collect information from your device.
Passwords are still important. However, they are only one part of the security system protecting your identity. Here are six ways criminals may try to get around traditional password protection and the practical steps you can take to protect yourself.
Join our CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money
In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us today, Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Missed this morning’s live class? Register at CyberGuyLive.com to watch the replay.
YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES
Cybercriminals can access online accounts without stealing passwords by hijacking login sessions, exploiting security approvals or abusing connected apps. (Photo by Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
When you sign in to a website, the service often creates a session that tells it you have already proved who you are. Your browser or app may keep that session active so you do not have to enter your password every few minutes. Criminals can sometimes steal the digital tokens or cookies associated with these sessions. If the service accepts the stolen information, an attacker may gain access without entering your password or completing another verification step.
How to protect yourself: Review the devices and active sessions connected to your accounts. Sign out of anything you don't recognize and check for suspicious login activity. We've previously explained how to check for unfamiliar devices and remove them from your Apple, Google and Microsoft accounts. If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and revoke other sessions when the service allows it. Remember that removing a device from an account list does not always terminate an active login session.
Your phone number is often connected to email, banking, payment and social media accounts. Criminals may try to convince a mobile carrier to transfer your number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. If the transfer succeeds, they may receive calls and text messages intended for you, including certain account verification codes. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign, especially when there is no known local outage. Other signs include an unexpected carrier notification about a device change or a password-reset message you did not request.
How to protect yourself: Ask your carrier about an account security PIN, number transfer lock and port-out protection. These protections vary by carrier. For sensitive accounts, use a passkey, security key or authenticator app when available. Unlike text verification codes, authenticator app codes generally do not depend on your phone number. If text messages are your only available second authentication method, keep them enabled. They still provide more protection than relying on a password alone.
ARE BANK TEXT CODES ENOUGH TO PROTECT YOU?
Stolen session cookies and malicious browser extensions can give hackers access to sensitive accounts, even when strong passwords are in place. (Photo by Britta Pedersen/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds another layer of protection to your accounts. However, criminals sometimes target the person receiving the security request. One tactic is MFA fatigue, also called push bombing. An attacker who can trigger authentication requests repeatedly sends approval notifications, hoping you eventually tap "Approve" to make them stop. Criminals may also impersonate technical support or a financial institution and ask you to read aloud a one-time security code.
How to protect yourself: Never approve a login you did not initiate or share a verification code with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. If repeated prompts appear, deny them and check the account through its official website or app. Change your password if you suspect it has been compromised. When available, choose phishing-resistant authentication, such as a passkey or security key. App-based approvals that require number matching can also offer additional protection against accidental approvals.
An infostealer is malicious software designed to collect information from a device. Depending on its capabilities, it may steal browser-stored passwords, session cookies, payment information or other sensitive data. These programs can arrive through fake software updates, pirated applications, suspicious email attachments, malicious advertisements or compromised browser extensions. Some malware operates quietly, which means you may not immediately notice anything unusual.
How to protect yourself: Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated. Avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites and review browser extensions regularly. If you suspect malware has compromised a device, use a separate, trusted device to secure important accounts. Run a security scan with strong antivirus software and remove suspicious software. For a serious infection, professional assistance or reinstalling the operating system may be necessary. Avoid signing back into sensitive accounts until you are confident the device is secure.
Some criminals do not need to steal your password or infect your device. Instead, they may trick you into giving a connected application permission to access your information. For example, a fake productivity tool might ask to read your email, access your contacts or manage files in your cloud storage. You may encounter a legitimate-looking permission screen asking you to approve those requests. If you grant access to a malicious app, it may be able to retrieve information through the permissions you approved. In certain cases, that access can continue even after you change your account password. This technique is sometimes called OAuth consent phishing. In a September 2026 warning, the FBI explained that criminals can trick people into granting malicious applications access to their accounts. That access can remain active even after a password change unless the victim revokes the application's permissions.
How to protect yourself: Review the third-party applications connected to your Google, Microsoft and other important accounts. Look closely at what each application can access. Remove permissions for apps you no longer use or do not recognize. Be especially careful with applications requesting access to email, contacts, cloud files or account management features.
Passkeys can significantly reduce the risk of traditional password phishing. They use cryptographic credentials associated with your device, security key or password manager. Unlike a password that you type into a website, a properly implemented passkey is tied to the legitimate website or service. That makes it much harder for a fake login page to steal the credential. However, passkeys do not eliminate every security risk. Criminals may still target an already authenticated session, an infected device, a malicious connected application or an account recovery process.
How to protect yourself: Use passkeys when your important accounts support them. Protect your devices with a strong screen lock and keep recovery information current.

articles.title_orig: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
articles.title_zh: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
articles.content_orig:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said Saturday that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Khamenei made the remark on X after meeting with senior commanders of the Iranian military.
"Should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end," he wrote.
"The military target database must be updated comprehensively to ensure that all kinds of physical and non-physical assets" of the U.S. and Israel "are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," Khamenei also said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump "hasn't made a decision" whether or not to resume strikes on Iran.
Rubio, speaking at the G20 meeting in Atlanta, said Trump prefers to solve the conflict diplomatically.
"This is also a country and a regime that is at the center of all the instability in the Middle East," Rubio said earlier. "In Lebanon there is instability because they support Hezbollah. In Saudi Arabia they are under attack because Iran supports the Houthis. In Iraq, is a country that is feeling challenged because Iranian-backed militias are challenging the state there. So anywhere you turn what you find is some Iranian proxy that's undermining the peace and stability of the Middle East. That is a fundamental threat that we have to confront, on top of the fact that they want nuclear weapons."
"This is a regime that has massacred its own people," he added. "You could only imagine what it would do to others if it possessed weapons of mass destruction, which will never be allowed to happen as long as President Trump is in the White House."
Strikes launched by Iran against more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East have resulted in billions of dollars of equipment damage, according to The Associated Press.
The news agency cited its analysis on satellite imagery from multiple providers and said it spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit.
The AP reported that through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with American equipment. Many of the attacks focused on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes, the AP added.
It said most of the Iranian attacks have been in Kuwait, but U.S. sites in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates also have been targeted.
Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait was struck at least 30 times, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to the AP.
This satellite image taken over Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait on July 24, 2026, shows the result of numerous strikes on this section of the bas. (Airbus DS 2026 via AP)
Al Dhafra Air Base, about 20 miles south of Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, was hit frequently early in the war, a regional military official with direct knowledge of the damage told the AP. The official noted damage to infrastructure like aircraft hangars and other installations as well as to equipment such as an early-warning radar system and surveillance drones.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told the AP that U.S. “forces and bases are well protected and America’s military is stronger than ever.”
“Our service members in CENTCOM have everything they need to continue their historic success ensuring Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon,” he added.
The Associated Press contributed to this post.
Major Gen. Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of the armed forces of Iran, insisted Saturday that the country's military would respond quickly to any attacks.
"Whenever signs of hostile enemy action are confirmed, the armed forces will not wait for the start of his action in choosing the time and manner of response," he wrote on X.
"With all informational capacity, we monitor the enemy's movements and preparations and update the target bank," Abdollahi added.
He made the remark in response to a call from Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to confront any threat "with an immediate, effective, and unrestricted geographical response."
Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Tehran currently has no plans to meet with U.S. officials for talks aimed at ending the war.
“We see no need to meet with the Americans at present. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them,” Araghchi reportedly said, adding, “What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation.”
The remarks come after an official told Reuters Saturday that Iranian negotiators are meeting with Qatari mediators in Doha.
The Qatari team has been in frequent contact with the U.S. during the discussions, Reuters cited an official briefed on the negotiations as saying.
Negotiators from Iran are in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday for talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the U.S.-Iran war, according to Reuters.
The Qatari team has been in frequent contact with the U.S. during the discussions, it cited an official briefed on the negotiations as saying.
The official added that Saturday's talks come after more than 12 hours of negotiations in Tehran, Iran, on Friday.
The U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran on Feb. 28.
Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs Waleed ElKhereiji said Saturday that people "want to bring peace back to the region" during the U.S.-Iran war.
ElKhereiji made the remark during the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) Manama Dialogue in Bahrain, where he added that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the conflict with Iran.
“If you look at… the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear," ElKhereiji said, according to The Associated Press. "People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region."
The Associated Press contributed to this post.
U.S. Central Command released a new image Saturday of a F/A-18 Super Hornet jet on the flight deck of the USS George H.W. Bush during nighttime operations.
The aircraft carrier has operated in the Middle East in support of the U.S. military's blockade on Iranian ports.
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said this week that "since day one, America's sons and daughters, serving in the Middle East, have shown relentless commitment, dedication, and courage.
"It's been the honor of a lifetime to serve alongside them and recognize them for the tremendous accomplishments on behalf of the nation," Cooper added. "As their commander, I could not be prouder, and I know that the families, friends, loved ones, and the American people back home share in this pride."
The Trump administration warned Iran that there "will be consequences" if Tehran continues its malign activities amid growing concern over a potential new round of U.S.-Iran hostilities after the midterm elections.
With just days until the 2026 elections and with war raging on in the Middle East, foreign ministers from the world's largest economies gathered in Atlanta, Georgia ahead of the G20 leaders meeting in December.
"The Iranian regime has had a choice... to either pursue the path towards normalcy, towards prosperity for their people, the path towards diplomacy. Or they can continue their malign activities, but there will be consequences for that, and we've seen the president taking concrete action," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital on Friday.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
articles.title_zh: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed puts ministers through military training
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.
Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.
The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.
Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.
It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.
In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.
He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.
"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.
Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.
The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.
It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.
Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

articles.title_orig: Gadi Eisenkot is the bereaved general trying to outmaneuver Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Gadi Eisenkot is the bereaved general trying to outmaneuver Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections .
Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
So how could a new government be formed?
Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible.
Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls.
Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that.
On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle.
Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office.
Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged.
Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc.
Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Eisenkot , however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind.
Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers.
But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar.
While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament.
Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first.
Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed.
If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out.
After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition.
If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election.
The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed.
A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years.

articles.title_orig: Iran Braces for More War, No Matter the Outcome of the U.S. and Israeli Elections
articles.title_zh: Iran Braces for More War, No Matter the Outcome of the U.S. and Israeli Elections
articles.content_orig:
Akhtar is a foreign correspondent for The Telegraph based in London
Iran is preparing to disrupt the US midterm elections after attempting to interfere in Israel’s vote this week , The Telegraph can reveal.
Several Iranian officials said Tehran viewed the near-simultaneous elections of its two biggest enemies as a rare opportunity to exploit vulnerabilities in their democratic systems.
“We have been looking into ways to recruit agents in both the American and Israeli regimes’ election processes,” one official said. He added that “powerful cyber groups have also been established to hack their election systems”.
Another official framed the effort as the natural extension of a war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
“War does not just mean missiles and guns when we are under their blockade,” he said.
“It also means we are prepared to disrupt their elections, their banking, their travel and all their ordinary systems. We are not in favour of any candidate anywhere, but we would like to see a divided America and a divided Israel .”
That, in the end, is Tehran’s prize.
Eight months into the on-and-off conflict, Tehran has concluded that the surest route to relief runs not through the battlefield but through the voting booths of Tel Aviv and Washington – hoping, in effect, that voters will do what its missiles could not.
Publicly, Iranian officials show contempt for the elections.
Asked about the Israeli election , Esmail Baghaei, the foreign ministry spokesman, likened it to the Cold War satire Dr Strangelove.
“I don’t think there’s really an election there,” he told reporters in Tehran on Monday. “It’s a competition between rival gangs over who can commit more evil – a contest over who can kill more.”
It made no difference, he added, “who ends up at the helm of a regime whose only achievement for our region has been killing and violence”.
Privately, however, the calculation is colder and more confident.
“For us it does not matter who wins or who loses any of the elections in America or Israel,” a third senior Iranian official told The Telegraph.
“Whoever wins in Israel , they will still be the enemy. And in America, it would be good to see voters, who are angry at their warmonger ruler, make a decision that would bring peace to the world.”
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, was pushing for renewed strikes on Iran in the run-up to the election, according to reports.
He frequently warned that Israel might face annihilation at the hands of Tehran if his time as prime minister ended.
But the Iranian official warned that any renewed assault would be met more broadly than before.
“In Tehran, we are not sitting and waiting for their election results, and we are in charge of the war,” he said.
“Ready to make meaningful peace, and ready for a harsh response – and our reaction will not be limited only to American assets, like the previous time.”
In Israel, the thing Tehran wants most is paralysis.
A government consumed by coalition haggling and domestic reckoning is a distracted one, buying Iran time to rebuild the missile and air defence stocks damaged by this year’s strikes.
A deadlocked result could leave a caretaker government with no mandate for a major new offensive, or force a repeat election that freezes decisions for months.
Dr Steven Wagner, a senior lecturer in international security at Brunel University of London, said Iran had good reason to watch and wait rather than act.
“I would expect Iran has been hoping for Netanyahu to lose, and for the criminal proceedings against him to disqualify him from future office,” he said.
“We won’t know what will happen in Israel for a few days, as forming a government takes time, and Bibi is very likely to use every second of it and attempt to stall.”
Mr Netanyahu’s opponents, Mr Wagner said, faced their own dilemmas, “whether to go back on promises and form a coalition with Arab parties,” and whether Gadi Eisenkot , the prime minister’s leading rival, would accept “a path to end the war in Gaza, or a crackdown on settler violence”.
He added: “From Iran’s point of view, there is plenty of time to wait and see what happens, to continue to consolidate what hasn’t been destroyed and to bolster defences where they need to.
“I would not expect any major action from Iran under the circumstances, as it would disturb their very good chances for favourable outcomes in both cases.”
Iranian officials have followed the mechanics of the Israeli elections closely. As it stands, neither the pro-Netanyahu or anti-Netanyahu bloc has enough seats to form a majority.
With nearly 86 per cent of votes tallied on Wednesday, Israel’s three main broadcasters projected Netanyahu’s bloc of Right-wing, far-Right and ultra-Orthodox parties would win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, well ahead of the 48 for rival Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.
Parties representing Arab Israelis were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Mr Eisenkot little realistic path to power without their broad backing – which many Jewish political leaders reject.
Fada Hossein Maleki, a member of the national security and foreign policy committee in the Iranian parliament, said the Arab parties were pursuing two goals: blocking a victory for Mr Netanyahu and winning enough seats to shape the formation of the next government.
“Although the Arab parties do not by themselves have the seats to form a government, in a situation where none of the rival camps can secure a majority, even a limited number of seats can prove decisive,” he said.
Netanyahu will not ally with them, Mr Maleki said, and Mr Eisenkot faces his own constraints, since a formal pact with Arab parties “could cause part of his voter base to waver”.
If no deal is reached, he warned, “the likelihood of continued political deadlock rises” and with it the chance of a fresh election “that could place greater political and administrative pressure on the regime in the middle of a war”.
It is Washington, however, where Iranian optimism runs highest.
The midterm elections on Nov 3 will decide control of the House and a third of the Senate. Tehran is betting they will clip Donald Trump’s wings and return Democrats to Congress, restraining what one official called the US president’s “madness”.
Dr Wagner said: “Iran will be looking at the US midterms for signals that Congress might restrain the White House’s spending on the war and on Israel.”
Amir Ali Abolfath, an Iranian analyst of American affairs, laid out why Tehran has hopes – and why it should temper them.
Three indicators, he said, point the same way – the tradition that a ruling party loses ground in its first midterm, which “works against the Republicans”; polling that gives Democrats the better chance in the House, and betting markets that put their odds of taking the House at “around 75 to 80 per cent”.
The Senate race “is a harder contest” Mr Abolfath said, with the markets offering the Democrats a 60 per cent chance of victory. But Republicans “have thrown everything into holding the Senate”, and a hostile Congress would not by itself halt the war.
“A Congress not aligned with the president can create obstacles and headaches,” he said, “but one should not imagine that a Democratic victory alone would prevent war, because they do not fully hold that power, and the US president, as commander-in-chief, has considerable authority to launch or resume an attack.”
Mr Abolfath warned that the vote could accelerate, rather than delay, a new strike on Iran.
The White House might calculate that it could “end the war in three or four days”, and declare on the eve of the election that it had forced Iran to surrender, handing the Republicans a victory, he said.
He added: “But if American decision-makers conclude that this scenario will not materialise – that, as in the 40-day war, Iran will resist and the war will drag on with greater intensity and regional consequences – they may not be willing to risk starting a conflict on the e

articles.title_orig: Taipei mayor gets angry reception at Pride after gay bar raid
articles.title_zh: Taipei mayor gets angry reception at Pride after gay bar raid
articles.content_orig:
The rounding up of customers at a gay bar weeks before Saturday’s Pride festival has some questioning the island’s progressive image
J osh was having a drink at Commander D, a popular gay bar in Taipei, on a Saturday afternoon when several police officers suddenly burst in. “Squat down and don’t move,” they shouted. Bewildered, he looked around to see the bar owner being handcuffed and forced to his knees.
The 28-year-old was among 51 customers to be rounded up and taken away for questioning over suspected breaches of public decency rules.
“I didn’t expect something like this to still happen these days. It definitely made me feel a lot less safe,” says Josh, a gay man from Taiwan whose name has been changed due to the sensitivity of the incident. The police operation was criticised by rights groups as heavy-handed, and has unsettled LGBTQ+ communities in Taiwan.
On Saturday the island hosts one of the region’s largest Pride parades , and some say the police operation is emblematic of a persistent, wider stigma that risks jeopardising its global image as a LGBTQ -friendly destination.
The raid took place on 3 October at a bar that is billed as Taipei’s first and only BDSM-themed bar and features in several international travel guides. Commander D has operated for more than a decade in the Ximending area – a hub for LGBTQ+ tourists where gay bars and sex shops can be easily spotted.
The bar’s owner was arrested and referred to prosecutors on suspicion of profiting from facilitating sexual or indecent acts, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison.
In the days after the raid, the police department said that it had received 13 complaints this year alleging public decency violations at the bar.
In an interview with Taiwanese media on 7 October, the bar owner accused the police of using excessive force and said that any intimate encounters between customers were a matter of personal choice. He has not yet been formally charged with any offences. His lawyer declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing investigation.
Videos posted on social media showed the police mocking a disabled customer and preventing some people from putting their clothes back on. Some had taken their shirts off because it was a warm day. Police said they had reviewed 41 body cam recordings and acknowledged inappropriate language had been used by its officers.
“There was an element of sexual humiliation,” says Victoria Hsu, a human rights lawyer specialising in LGBTQ+ rights. As police refused to let the patrons get dressed, “they weren’t allowed to go to the police station with dignity”.
The police department said their actions were intended to bring the scene under control and the court-authorised search had not targeted any particular group or sexual orientation. Yet after a strong public backlash, Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an apologised and six police officers were disciplined for inappropriate remarks and failing to supervise their juniors properly. Rights groups are calling for an independent investigation.
Wanhua police division said rights groups filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors on 7 October. “The matter has entered the judicial process, and we await the outcome of the investigation and any subsequent court proceedings.”
Midnight Poonkasetwattana, executive director of the Bangkok-based LGBTQ+ advocacy network APCOM, told Taiwan’s Central news agency that the raid “could undermine the gay-friendly image Taiwan has built”.
Hung Yan-an, a gay man living in Taipei, says he received messages from overseas friends about the incident. “A gay friend of mine in Spain has been asking me: ‘Is everything OK? If I visit, will it be safe to hold hands with my partner in the street?’”
The episode stands in stark contrast to a recent survey that found public support for gay marriage has increased from 42% to 54% since Taiwan legalised same-sex marriage in 2019, the first place in Asia to do so.
“But inclusion is not only about marriage equality, Pride or international recognition. It is also about how public institutions treat LGBTQI+ people when exercising state power,” Poonkasetwattana said in a formal letter of protest to Taiwan’s representative in Thailand over the decision to raid Commander D.
Local campaigners say the raid exposes a persistent stigma around queer venues, as well as “homophobia, discrimination and abuse of power that have long been embedded in the police system”.
A spokesperson for the Wanhua police division did not directly address the allegations of longstanding institutional homophobia but said it “fully respects social and cultural diversity and people’s rights” and would continue to combat crime and enforce the law to maintain public order.
Other gay venues have also faced scrutiny. In April, a gay bathhouse in the central city of Taichung closed after a police raid over suspected public-decency offences and subsequent inspections. In a Facebook statement announcing the closure, its owner accused police of discriminatory treatment. A gay gym in Taipei, which closed in 2021, had reportedly been inspected 186 times over three years.
“Some police officers assume that gay people are more likely to have drugs on them,” lawyer Hsu says. “I’ve had quite a few LGBTQ+ people come to me for legal advice, for example, some of them were subjected to improper police searches.”
For Chien Shih-han, a Taiwanese drag queen who performs as Hannah, discrimination is not always easy to identify. He recalls gay venues facing repeated noise complaints and a pre-booked taxi driving away after the driver saw a friend in drag.
“It could all come down to this subtle sense of discomfort or anxiety towards sexual minorities,” Chien says.
In his view, gay venues such as Commander D have offered a refuge to people who do not fit the mainstream, even within the LGBTQ+ community. “It was a kind of safety net,” Chien says. “Now it feels as though someone is setting fire to that net.”
Weeks later, Josh says he still feels “a little scared” when thinking back to the raid, but that it would not stop him taking to the streets for Taiwan Pride.
“I want to express my anger at being taken to the police station that day,” he says, “I want to go with the message that we’re not strange, we’re not freaks.”

articles.title_orig: Train Disaster Is Blow to Spain’s Leader, Already Election Underdog
articles.title_zh: Train Disaster Is Blow to Spain’s Leader, Already Election Underdog
articles.content_orig:
Pedro Sanchez, the Spanish prime minister, has called a snap election for 29 November following large-scale housing protests across the country. A month out from the election, new YouGov data sets the scene as the country weighs up its options.
Unsurprisingly, given the ongoing protests, Spanish people are most likely to pick housing as a top issue facing the country, with over half (53%) choosing it as one of their top two most important issues.
Housing substantially outstrips all other issues, with the next highest issue – the level of immigration – chosen by 35%. Corruption and fraud follow in third place, on 28%.
A further 19% cite the healthcare system, while 15% choose the general state of the economy. All other options are chosen by fewer than 10% of Spaniards.
Looking at how people intend to vote in the upcoming election shows a clear divide.
Those who say they are voting for the Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), led by Pedro Sánchez, cite housing as the biggest issue (69%), followed by healthcare (31%). Voters for the smaller left-wing Broad Front (FA) rank the issues similarly, with 73% choosing housing, 31% the healthcare system, and 25% the gap between the rich and poor.
While housing is still a key issue for voters intending to back right-wing parties, they are much less likely to choose it than their left-wing counterparts. Those who are voting for the centre-right People’s Party (PP) are similarly likely to choose either housing (49%) or immigration (44%) as top issues facing Spain, with 39% picking corruption. Housing places third for far-right Vox voters, at 31%, with this group instead much more likely to choose immigration (68%) and corruption (41%).
We also asked 2,175 Spaniards to tell us, in their own words, what is most influencing their decision to vote and who to vote for. We categorised the responses using our AI-powered topic quantifier model, with the results showing that the biggest factor driving decisions to vote is stopping a right-wing government (14%), followed by desire for a change of government (9%) and the issue of corruption (8%).
Opposition to a potential PP-Vox government is a major motivator on the left, with 39% of current PSOE voters saying that avoiding a right-wing government is the biggest influence on their vote.
The picture is reversed on the right: 22% of current PP voters and 15% of Vox voters cite the need for a change of government. Voters for right-wing parties are also far more likely than those who are backing left-wing parties to mention corruption – 16% and 12% among PP and Vox voters, compared to 1% among PSOE voters.
When it comes to specific policy areas, housing (7%) and immigration (6%) are the ones Spaniards mention most. Housing is brought up most often by young people: 12% of 18-24 year olds cited it in their answers, compared to 5% of the over-50s, reflecting the impact of the housing crisis being felt more keenly by young people in Spain.
Immigration is brought up most frequently by Vox voters, with a fifth (21%) citing it as the biggest influence on their vote, compared to 6% among PP voters and only 1% of PSOE voters.

articles.title_orig: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.title_zh: Yes, Alphabet Stock Got Hammered. No, We’re Not Selling.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Big Tech's brutal week had one clear epicenter. Alphabet ( GOOGL ) lost $468 billion in market value this week, more than SpaceX, Intel and Nvidia combined.
That was the Google parent's worst week ever and the second-biggest weekly wipeout for any US-listed stock, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $552 billion in the week of Jan. 27, 2025, when China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Alphabet's previous worst was about $386 billion in the week ended June 26.
Most of the damage came Thursday, when Alphabet lost $475 billion in a single session after its third quarter results . Friday's slide wiped out the gains the stock had made earlier in the week.
October was even worse. Alphabet shed about $758 billion in market value this month, the second-biggest monthly loss ever for a US-listed company. Only SpaceX ( SPCX ) has lost more, about $822 billion in July. Alphabet's October loss is nearly double its previous worst month, about $420 billion in February 2025.
In percentage terms, the stock fell nearly 19% in October, its worst month since it went public in 2004. Its previous worst was an 18.5% drop in November 2008. For the week, it fell nearly 13%, its worst since August 2011.
The selloff has left Alphabet's price-to-earnings ratio at its lowest in more than a decade .
SpaceX, Intel ( INTC ) and Nvidia each lost more than $100 billion in market value this week. Intel fell as much as 30% Friday after a weak outlook, its steepest drop in decades . Amazon ( AMZN ) shed about $80 billion for the week after reporting results Thursday. Some software names fell harder in percentage terms, with ServiceNow ( NOW ) and Fortinet ( FTNT ) down roughly 25% to 34%.
Not all of that money left the market. Eli Lilly ( LLY ), Tesla ( TSLA ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) added more than $300 billion in combined value, even as the Magnificent 7 stumbled .
UBS's chief investment office argued against heading for the exits. "Further volatility does not make retreating from markets an effective way to protect portfolios from potential drawdowns, in our view," Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities, wrote Friday. "We continue to see scope for equity gains overall and believe investors should focus on building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech."
The close settled it. October goes down as Alphabet's worst month since its IPO, in dollars and in percentage terms. The stock finished the week about $7 above the roughly $273 level it would have needed to take Nvidia's weekly record.

articles.content_orig:
CNBC's Jim Cramer warned on Friday that volatility on Wall Street may not be over.
Stocks endured a turbulent week as renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade weighed on technology shares. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.3% through Wednesday before plunging 2.9% Friday, ending the week down 2%. The S&P 500 followed a similar pattern, rising 1.6% through Wednesday before tumbling 1.8% Friday to finish the week down 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average also reversed course, gaining 0.5% through Wednesday before slipping 1.1% Friday to end the week down 0.9%.
"After a brutal week for tech, don't assume the worst is behind us," the " Mad Money " host said. "We've got the election, uncertainty overseas, the jobs report and another slew of earnings."
"My advice?" he added. "Don't try to call the bottom in the Nasdaq just yet. Pick up some high-quality companies that are being thrown away, and remember, in this market, even great earnings might not be enough to send a stock higher."
With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead.
Apple reports after the bell. Shares recently hit an all-time high, helped by enthusiasm for its latest products, including the upcoming Duo foldable phone. Cramer remains bullish on the company but acknowledged that its valuation of almost 40 times earnings leaves little room for disappointment. "You can trade it, but I am going to own it," he said.
Cramer also expects encouraging results from Palantir when it reports, citing strong customer feedback about the value of its AI software.
The midterm elections take center stage, with Cramer watching whether a shift in congressional control could threaten planned data center projects. He warned that growing political opposition to the facilities could delay construction and hurt companies whose growth depends heavily on AI infrastructure spending. However, he's "not going to write off the data center entirely because there are plenty of states that will welcome them."
On the earnings front, Advanced Micro Devices reports, offering another important test for the semiconductor sector following Intel's disappointing results . Cramer expects AMD to report better numbers than rival Intel.
Drugmakers Pfizer and Amgen also report. Cramer said both could benefit from renewed investor enthusiasm for pharmaceutical stocks.
CVS Health reports, and Cramer remains intrigued by the company's position in the healthcare sector. However, he expressed concerns about its pharmacy benefit management business. "I wish it could disengage with that business; its stock would go higher," he said.
McDonald's earnings will also be in focus. Cramer wants to see whether the company's restaurant improvement strategy is gaining traction amid reported concerns from franchisees.
Kimberly-Clark reports, with Cramer optimistic about the consumer products company's prospects following its planned merger with Kenvue . The stock has benefited from investors rotating into consumer staples, and Cramer remains bullish on the company. "If this one falls before then, I think you should pick some up," he said.
The monthly jobs report will provide another important test for markets. Cramer expects strong hiring but limited wage growth, a combination that could help ease inflation concerns and explain the relative stability in Treasury yields.
The CNBC Investing Club will also hold its annual meeting, where Cramer and Jeff Marks will discuss the portfolio, market risks and their biggest investment winners.

articles.title_orig: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
articles.title_zh: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

“I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”
I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh !), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.
By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.
When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.
As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases . I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.
As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.
There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.
“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”
As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)
I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.
Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze.
Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing.
This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!)
In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo.
For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly.
Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like. If anything, the black-barred apps felt more like an aesthetic issue than a functional problem, even though they’re smaller than usual when the Duo is folded.
I expect all the major apps will eventually update. As for the older apps that never do? Well, it’s probably time to move on from apps no longer being maintained, I’d say, particularly in an era when older software is being exploited left and right by AI-enabled hacking tools.
However, I will agree with the other reviewers who complained about the lack of Face ID.
This is the Duo’s biggest drawback – not the screen, not the camera, not the lack of an Action button for launching your preferred AI assistant. It’s Touch ID.
It is much easier to look at your phone than to fiddle around with finger presses. While I easily avoided the need to use Touch ID to unlock the device – I am almost always wearing an Apple Watch, which serves as an alternative authentication method – I often stumbled when it came to using apps and Apple Pay.
Tap-and-pay is one of the areas where it’s immediately obvious how much smoother Face ID has made everyday tasks. Returning to Touch ID at the time of payment was cumbersome, given that you’re often holding shopping bags, a purse, and, in my case, a dog leash, in addition to the phone you’re using to pay with.
There’s a certain amount of what I guess I’ll call “muscle memory” that you have to overcome when you switch back to Touch ID. I found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone in your hand and use your thumb to authenticate. But where I repeatedly messed up was remembering to keep my thumb or finger on the Touch ID sensor long enough to authenticate. At times, my finger wasn’t situated quite right (I blame the dog pulling on the leash!), and I had to readjust. “I miss Face ID!,” I complained multiple times at checkout.
Though returning to Touch ID was something I got used to, it’s far from ideal. I can see this as being a real stopping point for some early adopters who would otherwise want to move to the Duo. It’s not an insurmountable problem, but it’s among the top reasons not to get the Duo now, in my opinion. (A future version is said to support Face ID .)
Another reason to be wary of the Duo? The camera. Much has been said about the Duo’s lesser camera system. The Duo has two rear cameras to my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s three. It has no telephoto lens. It has a 10x digital zoom versus the Pro’s 40x. The Pro has more advanced hardware for low-light photography and supports ProRAW, ProRes, and other advanced features.
Very simply put: if you are an iPhone photographer or a content creator, you shouldn’t consider the Duo as your primary device.
For, you know, us normal folks, the Duo’s camera is okay. Not great, but fine. What were you going to do with those photos you’re snapping anyway? Post them to Instagram Stories or Facebook? Text them to a friend? Look back on them fondly when they reappear in your photo widget on your Home Screen? Turn them into a Lock Screen wallpaper? None of these things requires a Pro-level camera.
